title: 软件开发走向智能体化后，如何判断质量？Emily Bache 与 Sam Newman 对谈
author: Modern Software Engineering
content:
Brief Description

Emily Bache and Sam Newman discuss internal and external software quality, domain language, agent development loops, and why experienced engineers and testers remain essential.

Table of Contents

  • Internal and external quality
  • Domain language and acceptance tests
  • TDD and development loops
  • Making good changes explicit
  • Exploratory testing and human expertise
  • Augmentation and closing reflections

Internal and external quality

Welcome to One Big Question with me, Emily Bache, and with Sam Newman. This question we're discussing today is what does quality look like when software development becomes agentic?

Sam Newman: It's kind of It's an interesting question, like my Okay, this is my knee-jerk reaction to the question, which we can kind of you can see we disagree or we can go further, which is I don't think the end user definition of quality has changed at all. I just think it's how we assess it has got different, like I mean unless I'm wrong or maybe people use software, they've got a different view of it now it's agentic. I don't know.

Emily Bache: Maybe they've got lower expectations.

Sam Newman: Yeah. Oh, I expect it to be rubbish and really expensive. I don't know, but it kind of feels like those fundamentals, like when I think about you know, the when someone says is this quality or not, it's like they're kind of talking about does it functionally work? Is it kind of quick and responsive enough?

Is my data safe? Is all these are kind of I don't know that has changed. But what seems to have got really difficult is us as software developers working out how the hell to make sure our software is good enough. That seems to be the really tricky part.

Emily Bache: Yeah, I mean there's also that discussion about distinguishing internal and external quality. Cuz I mean what you've been talking about here is the external quality, what the user perceives. and the internal quality is what the software developers perceive when they open up and look in the code.

Emily Bache: so you know, and now the code is largely being written by these agents. and it varies how much of the code people actually reading. but to the extent that people are reading the code, then that's where the paying attention to internal quality comes in, I guess.

Sam Newman: Yeah, I think that's fair. I mean, we could even break I guess I had this conversation with Kevlin a while ago. We could probably even break that internal quality into two parts, which is kind of operational quality, which would might be about resiliency and you know, availability and stuff. And then that developer experience, right?

What's it like to actually spend time in this code or with this architecture? And so I think like yeah, looking at through that kind of yeah, experiential lens. I think that's absolutely fair. There's this big conversation.

I was just at a conference. I was at FastFlow Conf yesterday in London. It was a great event, but lots of people having this conversation as has been the case for all the events I've been at this year, which is do I need to look at the code anymore?

And does that matter? And I suspect where whether or not you're a company where you actively look at the code and engage with it on a day-to-day basis, you probably have a very different set of requirements about how or a different you might pay to different degree of importance on what that code is like to work with than maybe an organization which is maybe operating at a different level of abstraction where they're they're really caring a bit more about maybe there's operational and external character you know, quality characteristics and what the code looks like is less important if you don't look at it.

Emily Bache: Right. Well, even if humans don't look at the code, agents are looking at the code and it seems to be the case that the if the code quality is poor that the agents take a lot more tokens. And so it costs more, it takes longer, and they're more likely to make mistakes.

Sam Newman: I think that for me is like really interesting. So I think like the question then is are there different quality attributes that AI coding agents care about than humans? There's an overlap, which I think is good, but are there different characteristics of importance to those two groups?

Emily Bache: At the moment, it I don't think we know. I mean, there's so much here we don't know. We're kind of speculating. and the research is not keeping up with the with the state of the art. So it's hard to make definitive claims there, but for the kinds of teams I'm working with, they are still reading the code.

So it what works for humans seem to also help agents and that's a good starting point.

Domain language and acceptance tests

Sam Newman: Well, that's one thing that immediately makes sense to me that would be applied equally for humans and for agents is the words we use in the code. So, what we call a function, a class, or whatever else because say you are even are operating at that high level of abstraction, you're going to say something like when we send an order, make sure we also trigger an email or whatever you might say. You're you're pretty communicating with it with terms from the domain. And if those words aren't in the code, like as a human being, we will I bet you know I'm sure we've worked in code bases where what the domain is bears no relation to what the code looks like, but we do that translation in our heads, right?

But AI can't. So, if that meaning isn't in the code, that's great for the humans looking at it, but that's also great for AI, right?

Because we can talk in those terms. And that feels that feels really important still.

Emily Bache: Right. And so, those getting that domain language into the code comes from the way you've set up the requirements or the conversation with the agent about what it should build and what it should do. So, there's still a big part of this which is specification by example and good acceptance tests and all of that's where the domain language and setting that up in advance, I think, can come from.

Sam Newman: I've spoken to a few teams actually where they've you know, I mean I think I think this like reinforces the importance of domain-driven design in general, even if you're not going to buy the whole enchilada, right? The book's behind me. It's a thick book, right? But that aspect of getting the language out, I think, is really important because I think when we've got humans directly interacting with code, we can rely on a lot of tacit knowledge we've got in our heads, but we need to get it out now. and so, that for me kind of reinforces like the importance of doing something like an event storming exercise to bootstrap some of that language.

I've even spoken to some teams where they just can't get everyone in the room to have the conversation or they've got more disparate teams and they've been using things like the grill me skills to get information from people about how the language and the terms they use and I think those things are like really kind of just they they seem like no-brainer stuff to do anyway, right?

Because I think they help humans and they help the AI from that point of view and it also probably I'd imagine makes it easier to verify the behavior of your software in those terms as well, right? When you're doing say an acceptance test cuz then you could have a product owner like when you're working on a spec decide they could probably specify the acceptance criteria as an example in those languages as well. Is that You know more about acceptance testing than I do though.

Emily Bache: I think it yeah, I think you're on that's what I'm hearing as well that it's defining these tests having this domain driven design conversations and that's that's really helpful. I'm also finding that people are talking about the inner loop you know, where traditionally you'd have done TDD with the those very fine grained unit tests.

Sam Newman: Yeah.

Emily Bache: That that part of course to a large extent the agent is doing that part now. which is very big change and

TDD and development loops

Sam Newman: Yeah. I have a controversial view about TDD. I don't like being controversial by purpose but I love TDD but for me it was always about helping design the code and thinking is those small units and sort of I don't know that TDD has the same value now because we to your point that inner loop has gone to the agent.

Emily Bache: Yeah, and there's there's been I've made a video about this on the channel recently cuz there have been some high profile people saying, "Oh, I no longer do TDD." But I've been talking to a lot of people who are still finding that valuable because the internal code quality at the lowest level still seems valuable and TDD is one way that you can ensure that. If you're if you've got the these tight development loops going around every few minutes with No, it's it's the people who are doing this are not using a very naive kind of one paragraph TDD description. They they've got setups for this with perhaps sub subagents doing parts of it and very specific prompting and habit hooks or sensors that really ensure that the agent is refactoring frequently. So there is I think there's a still a discussion to be had about how to ensure that very low-level code quality

Emily Bache: and perhaps TDD is part of the answer there. But yes, it is different now.

Making good changes explicit

Sam Newman: There's something I seen quite a I was team from Finn in Ireland who's been purchased by Salesforce actually did a talk at Honeycomb's event last week and they were talking about the things that they do to avoid the requirement for a human to look at code. And they say, "A lot of our code doesn't have a human review now, but for us to get there we as a team had to say, 'This is what a good change looks like.' And you have to have passed those criteria. One of those criteria is the change set has to be below a certain number of lines of code. It might be 500 lines of code.

I might be making that number up, but they said, 'So you've got to pass all these gates, most of which are not AI involved automation test.' Like this like going through your lint you know, your linter and everything else and your static checks and things.

But like if this change is over 500 lines of code you have to have a human review. So you're incentivized to try and find a way to work with your AI to get it to be smaller changes. So they're trying to incentivize the right behavior. But if you do, then it can go straight in.

Their rationale being of course is you've made a smaller change. So if that no human review change has had a problem it can it's a small change to deal with, right? But and I kind of I think that was a nice and nuanced approach to I've got to look at every single line of code and I've got to artisanally created and type my own semicolons too. I'm just going to yolo the whole thing.

Whereas this is much more making again maybe it's coming back to making that tacit knowledge in our heads about what a good change looks like making that more explicit.

Which again helps the AI verify that it's writing code in the right way if it's executing your specs. But it also occurred to me that it also makes things more explicit for new people joining the team, right? This is what you've got to do. And I thought that was kind of interesting.

I mean they had to hand roll a lot of this internally but

Emily Bache: I think there's there's a there's a theme here about you need to know what good looks like.

Sam Newman: Yeah.

Emily Bache: For quality in agentic software you there's a certain amount of that this is all about augmenting human expertise. And it's the recurring theme for me is that all the people who are really doing agentic development successfully were already really skilled. Yeah, and really knew what good looked like and were good at engineering. And now they've got new tools to do that engineering with.

They can work even more effectively. So I I've also on the on the flip side you can see this where you've give these tools to people who have never written a good unit test in their life. And they're generating oodles of tests and they're basically worthless as far as I can tell. and that is easier than ever to do. So I think there's a real place for expertise.

Sam Newman: Absolutely. I mean I've seen a few presentations and spoken to a few people about how they're using specs and you don't have to dig very far to realize what they're basically doing is mini waterfall. Right? They're using the spec as as a sort of one shotting a spec that's say oh we'll spend a few weeks working on a spec as a team and then we'll implement the features like Okay, people we've done this before, right?

The time scales are different but the but the results are the results are very much going to be the same. And I think that thing you said though about knowing what good looks like is so important. I did a I don't know writing thing on a few weeks ago. I had a number of people talking who were doing sort of software factory stuff where they're quite hands-off or certainly heavily and some teams have been quite heavy specs based off and I had Yossi Matias there as well just before he joined Anthropic.

And every single one of them talked about you can't do this unless you can be specific about what good looks like. Because if you can't do that, the agent's not going to produce what you want. And so if you are creating things where you don't know what good looks like, where your understanding of this problem is a lot more vague, you're going to have to have a different kind of working model. Otherwise, this just isn't going to work.

And that kind of makes a lot of sense to me and I

Exploratory testing and human expertise

Emily Bache: Yeah. Can we can we talk about the the external quality? so we talked a little bit about the kind of other parts of this. The external quality is traditionally we've had a lot of manual testing for ensuring that, particularly around usability, you know. And now there are tools coming out that are able to do exploratory testing.

And in fact this episode is sponsored by Bear Queue, which is one of those tools. This episode is sponsored by Bear Queue from SmartBear. Its QA agents explore and map your application, create and maintain tests, validate real user journeys, and uncover coverage gaps that traditional scripts can miss.

As your product changes, Bear Queue adapts testing around how it works today, helping your team expand coverage, reduce script maintenance, and find real issues while maintaining control over the process.

Start your free Bear Queue trial today via the link in the description. And I just wanted to point out that this I think this could be amazing. but again, I'm I'm wanting to come back to that thing with expertise. If I'm not an expert exploratory tester, how can I tell if these things are actually doing it any doing any good? It's very easy to impress somebody who doesn't know anything.

Sam Newman: well, yeah, absolutely. And you know, I remember the early visual testing tools that came out, and it took experts to tell you that they were junk, right? Because they're based on pixel-perfect definitions and things like that. So, I am I think it's I mean, but also, let's look at this from a from an expert in the QA field or testing field, it's like the best QAs I've always worked with were able to look at like a portfolio of tests that you have around a system to say which parts of your system need more or less coverage. and even saying, "We've got too much coverage in this area.

It's not helpful. It's slowing us down." looking more holistically about what's happening. Like saying, "Okay, in production, we've had some issues in this area. Looking at it, we maybe could do with some more coverage around that."

So, the tools getting better, and certainly I can see the value, especially around some of the visual elements in helping and maybe even reducing some of the exploratory testing burden, which was often a bit more around some of the visualized elements potentially. but you still need that understanding of the balance of all of this. bear in mind, we're just talking about software, by the way, that is deterministic primarily in nature, right? That gets even more crazy once we start putting agentic software into production, right? Cuz at that point, then we've got the whole Yes, you need all that expertise that you've always needed with new tools, and they've got to understand how to use these new tools. Oh, and by the way, now we've got to start talking about Evals and sentiment analysis from people and trying to understand was that thumbs down on the response from your chatbot because the chatbot was broken and did something wrong, or was it because the chatbot was functioning correctly, it just gave the customer an answer they didn't like and so it's a whole like can of worms.

Emily Bache: that's definitely a huge can of worms when you start having agentic AI in your product. But even without that I'd guess I just want to deemphasize that I think you're going to get the best results with these kind of tools if you give them to really good engineers and see it as a way to augment them and give one person do more than if you're going to replace your whole QA with this with a tool. I think that's that's probably not going to work yet at least.

Augmentation and closing reflections

Sam Newman: I think it's also it's also kind of where the position of the human is in the system to an extent. Some of the kind of the mindset. I saw Cory Doctorow talk about this stuff a about 10 months ago. He was talking like in the context of radiologist.

You've got a radiologist who knows how to look at a scan and spot things. And there are two ways you could approach the value of AI in that world, right? The first is let's get rid of we've got six radiologists, let's get rid of five of them and then we'll have AI do the first pass of all the scans and then have the radiologist check them. And that's going to reduce our costs.

Right? But then you've basically got someone marking the homework of a computer. Or the other way to use it is no, we're going to add this capability to the radiologist we've already got and they're going to be like sitting on their shoulder going and you'll radiologist going through oh by the way, look at these spots or here's some areas I've highlighted for you.

Let's work together and work out where this is and that's probably going to lead to better outcomes. But back to your point like if you're seeing these new tools as a way of getting rid of people I think you're going to start losing the expertise you need to use those tools well. So I think it's like I would always like to position this more as these tools can help us do more things, can help us do some of the easier things so we can free up time to focus on the more interesting things.

Emily Bache: And that's that's always yeah, definitely. That's that's always been a theme in for testers looking at well, there's this cost to doing automation in terms of my time. And that's actually an opportunity cost cuz I'm spending time automating rather than exploring.

Sam Newman: Yeah.

Emily Bache: And what is the right balance? And the opportunity I think you get with these tools is that the automation time maybe goes down and gives you more time for that using your expertise effectively. So, that's what I would be looking for in these kinds of tools.

Sam Newman: And of course not only that, but you're going to need that additional bandwidth if you then plan to put AI agentic workflows into your products because suddenly I need to free up bandwidth to get my head around how we now verify these things that don't behave in the way that we, you know, traditionally expect, you know, code to have code to behave.

Emily Bache: We definitely live in interesting times.

Sam Newman: Yeah.

Emily Bache: Maybe this is the point to round off the discussion.

Sam Newman: Yeah, I think it's it's I think it's I really like the separation between the in the you know, the internal versus external quality. I think that's that's a nice framing around this as well. So, I I kind of like that, but yeah, hopefully this has been I think we were in violent disagreement. I don't know how interesting this makes this, but maybe we're in, you know, broad agreement about this.

Emily Bache: Yeah, maybe we're not quite aligned on TDD specifically.

Sam Newman: No, I like that. I I think I'm still working that through. Like, I like saying controversial things to myself to see if I really still believe things or not. So, we I you know, I'm just I'm going to hold fire on the explosive blog post on this until I've spoken to a few more teams, I think.

Emily Bache: It was great talking to you about this topic though anyway, Sam. Thank you.

Sam Newman: Yeah, thank you, Emily. And thank you also to Bear Queue for sponsoring the session. If you're interested in looking at some of the kind of new tools out there, go look at what SmartBear have got to offer and see how these new tools might help your QA spend more time on the hard things in life.

Emily Bache: Absolutely.
aiSummary: Emily Bache 与 Sam Newman 认为，智能体开发改变了质量验证方式，也让明确表达工程经验变得更重要。
oneSentenceSummary: Emily Bache 与 Sam Newman 认为，智能体开发改变了质量验证方式，也让明确表达工程经验变得更重要。
summary: Emily Bache 与 Sam Newman 区分用户体验到的外部质量，以及可运维性、代码工作体验等内部质量。领域语言、基于示例的规格和验收测试，可以帮助人与智能体对齐意图。两人对 TDD 的分歧保持克制：智能体正在接管内部实现循环，但精心设置的重构与测试仍可能保护底层设计。团队案例强调小变更和明确门槛，提到的 500 行阈值被明确标为不确定举例。他们提醒，长篇规格可能重演瀑布式开发，大量生成测试也不代表测试有价值。探索式测试部分含 BearQ 赞助，同时追问缺少经验的人如何判断工具效果。放射科类比说明，增强专家判断与替代专家会带来不同结果。自动化应释放工程师和测试人员的时间，用于更难的风险，尤其是产品开始包含非确定性 AI 时。

mainPoints.point: 区分用户结果与内部工程质量
mainPoints.explanation: 功能、响应速度与安全仍是用户关切；可运维性和代码体验则影响构建与运行软件的人。

mainPoints.point: 用领域语言明确隐性意图
mainPoints.explanation: 共同词汇、基于示例的规格与验收条件，帮助智能体使用与人相同的业务概念。

mainPoints.point: 保护反馈循环，避免无差别生成测试
mainPoints.explanation: 智能体接管实现后，TDD 的角色仍有争论；小变更与明确质量门槛仍需专业判断。

mainPoints.point: 用自动化增强专家能力
mainPoints.explanation: 探索式测试工具与 AI 生成测试都需要专业评估；替代专家可能同时移除判断结果所需的经验。

keyQuotes: 我认为用户对质量的定义完全没有改变。
因此我认为，专业经验仍然有很大的价值。
